To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the sialidase‐resistant receptors for species‐specific antibody on the human red cells are different from those of ABO and MN blood groups.
the species‐specific glycoproteins of human red cell membranes are resistant to sialidase and are not responsible for the ABO blood groups.
the species‐specific glycoproteins are sialoglycoprotein and that the receptors for species‐specific antihuman red cell serum are resistant to sialidase.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isolation of sialoglycoprotein from human red cell membrane and the study of their antigenic structure.
the species‐specific antigenic determinants on the red cell surface and the chemical basis for the antigenic determinants.
the sialoglycoconjugates of human red cell membrane.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sialoglyco‐protein is the receptor for species‐specific antihuman red cell serum and that the receptor for anti‐M or anti‐N sera is not identical with the species‐specific receptor.
the sialoglycopeptides are the receptors for the anti‐M and the anti‐N sera, but that the receptors for species‐specific antihuman sera are not identical with the sialoglycopeptides.
the sialoglycopeptides are the receptors for the specific antitoxin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the species‐specific glycoproteins of human red cells have receptors which are more resistant towards sialoglycoproteinase than those for anti‐M or anti‐N antibodies.

the sialoglycopolypeptide of the human red cell membrane is composed of two kinds of glycoprotein molecules: one with the receptor for the species‐ specific antiserum, the other with the receptors for anti‐M or anti‐N sera.

the species‐specific antigenic determinants are not located in the sialic acid‐containing oligosaccharide chains, and that the receptors for species‐specific antitoxins are located in the sialoglyco‐ proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use the specific antibody to isolate sialoglycoprotein from the membrane of human red cells.
the species‐specific glycoproteins of human red cells have a role in the species‐specific recognition of the red cells.
we have shown that there is an antigenic difference between the red blood cells of the different species.
